newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals-Cobalt price firm ahead of U.S. sales.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals-Cobalt price firm ahead of U.S. sales.

text.p: Cobalt prices were firmer in quiet Asian trade ahead of U.S. stockpile sales later this week, the first since March, Asian traders said on Tuesday.

"The upside is heavy. "It feels as if somebody is preventing them from moving upwards," said a trader at one of Japan's major trading houses. "But once the hands are removed, they're likely to climb again."
Traders said prices were firmer at $22.50/$23.00 per pound for high-grade cobalt and $19.50/$20.00 for low-grade metals.

They are now watching for the start of U.S. stockpile sales on Wednesday. The sale of 500,000 lbs of stockpiles will be the first one since the suspension in March following a lawsuit by Minor Metals Inc.

In the past, big traders have tried to push down the metal's price ahead of sales by the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) only to raise them after the bids, although the scope for such manipulation has been shrinking, they said.

Another trader, however, added: "Users are very cautious as they hope the prices will come down after the DLA sales. Only they have to continue purchasing more or less as their stocks reach only three months at the maximum."

A source close to a Zambian cobalt producer in Tokyo said the country's cobalt production was recovering towards a monthly level of 400 tonnes in August, up from 350 tonnes in July and a bottom of around 250 tonnes in March and April.
In the magnesium market, the price for Chinese metal was unchanged at $2,450/$2,500 per tonne, traders said.
However, they expect domestic prices to move higher during negotiations early next month for deliveries in the fourth quarter, partly to offset the dollar's advance against the yen.
"The price for the July-September quarter was based on the exchange rate of below 115 yen (per dollar). A change of two yen means a rise of five to six yen per kilo," said a trader.
But the trader added demand for beverage cans, which account for the lion's share of Japan's magnesium use, was smaller than expected, possibly because of overproduction in the previous quarter.
Prices for molybdenum oxide were also little changed at $4.45/$4.50 per pound as an increase in supply continued to be offset by strong demand, traders said.
While some traders forecast prices to come down towards $4.20 per pound during the summer holiday season, others saw little downside room due to the strong demand.
"There's no question Japanese demand is strong," said a trader. "Though the market's quiet, it doesn't make sense to sell the metal for lower prices."
Vanadium remained in tight supply, traders in Hong Kong and China said.
"There is sufficient supply in China for domestic consumption, but the export situation is not the same," a trader in Hong Kong said.
Vanadium pentoxide was quoted $4.05/4.10 per lb, she said, but her suppliers would not have any material available until August. Ferro vanadium (80 percent) was unavailable.
A Shanghai trader said vanadium pentoxide was being priced in China at $3.90/4.00 per lb, and he saw no impact on domestic supply due to tightness in the international market.

An official of the vanadium export department of Panzhihua Iron and Steel (Group) Corp, the country's biggest supplier of vanadium, said her company had not been affected by the market tightness because most of its production was exported anyway.

Panzhihua produced 83,334 tonnes of vanadium slag in 1996, up from around 52,000 tonnes in 1995, with the bulk of production exported, officials at the plant have said. -- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai Newsroom (8621) 6279-8544 -- Nao Nakanishi, Tokyo Commodities Desk +81-3-3432-7431
